vignette:
He is a 67-year-old widowed North American man who spent much of his adult life in military service as a medic, a role that taught him to move toward crisis rather than away from it. Before the collision, he prides himself on being steady under pressure, the kind of man who could focus while others panicked. He has been on roads, in convoys, and in emergency situations for years, and he has carried the memory of injury and death from his work without speaking much about it. Even after retirement, he remains the type to scan a room automatically, note exits, and think ahead to what could go wrong.

The motor vehicle collision happens on an ordinary day, which is part of what makes it so disorienting to him afterward. He is driving when another vehicle crosses into his lane, and in an instant the routine of the day turns into chaos. He remembers the violent impact, the sound of metal crushing, the sudden loss of control, and the frightening awareness that he may not survive. Time feels distorted in the aftermath. He is trapped, hurt, and overwhelmed by the realization that he cannot rely on the same calm, practiced response that usually carries him through emergencies. He later says that the worst part is not only the physical danger, but the helplessness of knowing this is happening to him rather than to someone he is trying to help.

In the days after the collision, he is shaken by how often the scene returns to him. At random moments he sees the flash of oncoming headlights, feels the jolt in his body, and hears the scrape and smash of the crash as if it is happening again. He becomes jumpy around traffic, especially at intersections, and he grips the steering wheel so tightly that his hands ache. He avoids driving when he can, then feels frustrated with himself for avoiding something that used to feel automatic. As a former medic, he knows how to manage pain and injury, but he is less prepared for the way his body stays on alert long after the wreck is over. He startles at sudden noises, struggles to settle at night, and finds himself checking the doors and windows more than he used to.

Sleep becomes one of the first things to go. He falls asleep reluctantly and wakes often, sometimes with his heart racing and an urgent sense that something bad is about to happen. On worse nights, he dreams of being pinned, unable to breathe, or of watching another person in danger while he cannot get to them in time. He wakes with a pounding chest and spends the rest of the night awake in the chair, staring at the television without taking in much of what is on the screen. He is embarrassed by how tired he feels and by how quickly his temper thins when he has not slept. Small frustrations, like someone driving too slowly or an unexpected phone call, can leave him irritated and tense.

He notices, too, that his world has narrowed. He turns down invitations more often and stays close to home, choosing familiar routes and familiar routines. He no longer trusts traffic the way he once did. Even when he is not directly thinking about the collision, his mind returns to it in fragments: the sound of the airbags, the smell of smoke, the helplessness in the moments afterward. Because he has spent a lifetime in military medicine, he is used to putting other people's needs ahead of his own, and he tends to minimize what he is going through. But in quieter moments, especially when he is alone, he feels a heavy mix of fear, grief, and disbelief that one crash has changed how he moves through the world.

His widowhood adds another layer of loneliness. His wife had been the person who could usually read his silences, notice when he was pushing too hard, and coax him back into conversation. Since her death, he has had to carry his distress more privately, and after the collision he feels that isolation more sharply. He does not easily ask for help, but he is aware that he is no longer the same man who once met danger with simple confidence. He is trying to continue with the routines of daily life, yet he does so carefully, as though the world is less predictable than it used to be and his body knows it before his mind can put it into words.
